utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. And may I say it's a pleasure to see Judge Lattanzi restored to us. And may I introduce, please, Kalin Stoyanov from Bulgaria, a law student here at The Hague who has been with my team since October of last year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Excellencies. Welcome, Honourable Judge Lattanzi. [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you were when the war broke out in Slovenia and Croatia. Where were you and what was your post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just understood. I wasn't in Slovenia when the war broke out. I was in another area when the war started in Slovenia. I've just now understood what you are asking. When the war broke out in Slovenia and Croatia, I was in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Han Pijesak. I was brigade commander, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which brigade was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the 216th Mountain Brigade. It belonged to the 4th Sarajevo Corps, and it was part of the then new system to the 2nd Military -- it was part of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned some difficulties in mobilisation yesterday, so we can skip that, but if you can just briefly tell us how the mobilisation proceeded in 1991, and how did the first mobilisation proceed and then the second one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember talking about problems. I just said that the brigade was mobilised. Therefore, yes, that is correct. As for this second part about problems, that is even more correct, I mean now that I hear it this morning. The brigade that I was in command of comprised 50 per cent of the Muslim population and 50 per cent of the Serb population. So it was a very rational structure, and it corresponded to the place, the area, that was -- that the troops were being drawn from. It was an excellent unit, and it was a good system until the -- the system of mobilisation or gathering the men broke down. The structure worked very well both as far as the civilian structure was concerned and as far as the military conscripts who manned the brigade. It all functioned very well. It was a very broad area around Srebrenica, Zvornik, Kladanj, Olovo, Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak. That was the territory that was being mobilised and where we drew our forces from. And then on the 30th of June, 1991, an order was issued on the mobilisation of the brigade, and then both -- members of both ethnic groups responded to the call-up, the Serbs and the Muslims. However, in the meantime, the Bosnia and Herzegovina leadership, in this case the Muslim part, issued instructions to their soldiers and to their population, their people, not to respond to the mobilisation, and then we had the situation in which I concluded actually these same soldiers were the ones who most regretted that this had happened. Some did obey that instruction or order. Many of them did not. So then there was a very difficult situation then for the survival of the brigade in that composition and also as far as the possibility of engaging the brigade in any kind of capacity. These conscripts, these soldiers, did not create any problems other than not responding, and those who did respond were loyal. Their conduct was normal. They could see that everything was all right. Later this escalated, so then a selection was made later so that later all of them left the unit and did not respond to the call-up any more for the brigade and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to give as brief answers as possible, although it's good to hear it all, but we do have a limited amount of time at our disposal. Who was authorised to order the mobilisation, and who issued the mobilisation order in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who issued the order to me, but who issued the order to them is something that I cannot confirm. I was given the order by the corps commander. There was a written order issued, and then the mobilisation got underway, that procedure got underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it in its full composition or was it the Rump Presidency, but did it have the authority to issue the mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a matter for the Yugoslav People's Army. So it wasn't the Territorial Defence that was being mobilised, but it also belonged to the whole of Yugoslavia, like the army did. So I assume that they did not have the authority to do that, because they interfered. And I know who they mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was your deputy? Who was the Chief of Staff of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is very specific. It is not just who was my Chief of Staff, if you permit me to say. The Chief of Staff specifically was Lieutenant-Colonel Asim Dzambasovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dzambasevic"]. However, the structure of the command, I would say, was absolutely multi-ethnic, and the chief of security was a Slovenian. The main operative officer was a Muslim. The chief of the technical service was Hungarian. It was a wonderful structure. It was a team that one could work with absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us how long these people stayed in the unit? When did Dzambasovic leave and when did the Slovenian and Hungarian leave and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Dzambasovic belonged to the type of people who were reasonable, educated, trained in the military sense, and he was just a normal man to work with and to co-operate with. I cannot specify exactly when he left. I cannot give you the date, but it was in that initial period. Actually, no, no. It was in 1992, 1992. If I'm not mistaken, it was in late 1991, early 1992. He asked in regular channels to leave to go to the corps command, to go and report to the corps commander and to see with him what would happen afterwards. I provided him with a vehicle. I provided him with staff to transport him. So it was a relationship of a civilised nature between people who respect each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were you and the unit when the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what happened with the unit while it was still part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this is a bit detailed to say where it was, I mean, it was in a number of places on a wide area, and in the context of the whole situation, at the point in time when the conflict became more serious and before we realised that the conflict would escalate, the brigade was in the Mesici sector. This is close to the Drina River. Raca or Praca and Visegrad, that's where we were, and we waited for a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did the brigade find itself in Sarajevo, on whose orders, and where was it deployed, and what were its tasks? It's a complex question, but I know that you will give us a detailed answer in any event.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, the brigade was in the Drina River Valley, in the area from Mesici to Visegrad. Along the depth it was in Rogatica sector and so on and so forth. At the point in time when - how shall I put it? - the escalation occurred or events that had to do with pulling out the column of the 2nd Military District command from Sarajevo and from the Bistrik area, that's when the situation began to become complicated. I had the impression that the corps commander made an assessment that the brigade should come to Sarajevo probably in order to assist in the withdrawal of the forces of the 2nd Military District. I'm not going to go into that. If somebody's in command, they know what their criteria are, and by getting there there was no way that we could help in any way this command of the 2nd Military District, even if we had helicopters and parachutes. So the brigade reached the Lukavica sector. The situation was underway with this column from Sarajevo. It was in progress. The column was cut in half. They fired at those people, and a part of the column -- I heard all of this, and I could see that it was going on. I could hear that it was going on. I couldn't see it. And then those who were wounded or killed there, nobody could help them, and those who in the meantime had managed to get out, they just said what had happened. And my brigade happened to be in the staging area in Lukavica without any fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was this brigade deployed later, and what happened to it when the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade was deployed in the Grbavica sector, a part of Lukavica, to Vraca and then up there the area below mount Trebevic or close to Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was the Jewish Cemetery also in the area of responsibility of the brigade, Bosut and the Jewish Cemetery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Bosut is a military facility, and it's a communications centre. It's a building with all the equipment and installations inside. There's no staff or personnel to defend it. Of course, the area of Bosut was supposed to be secured. I received an order to deploy a part of the forces to protect Bosut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened with the brigade when the JNA pulled out and when the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through the situation, because the cadres, the personnel, the officers who were in the brigade had come from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina and from outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were permitted to pull out and go back to Serbia or Montenegro, to that territory. I personally felt that there would be some difficulties and problems, considerable problems. However, we managed to deal with that by additionally engaging the existing cadre so that the command continuity of the forces could be maintained, and we adapted the structure to the given situation, to the conditions, and to the system of command which was possible to apply at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the brigade change its name, and did its area of responsibility change?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade was renamed after the divisions, and it was called now the 1st Romanija Brigade and was part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And my apology, I'm not sure I heard your second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the area of responsibility, did that change?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The area of responsibility remained as it was at the outset when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many battalions did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, the -- the team or the group, the entire unit, was a wonderful unit. You could use them in very difficult situations. The brigade was left without some battalions that had remained in the area, for instance, in Vlasenica. The brigade had two battalions, but we started a new recruitment procedure, mobilisation, from Sarajevo and Lukavica so that we replenished -- rather, brought up the personnel and manpower level to three battalions, and it existed in this form for a while. That's how it [indiscernible], but later on it grew and became a little bigger, and it was active in the wider area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when you arrived, what did you find there? With units in terms of the municipality, the area there, territorial units, what did you find? What situation did you find, and what happened with those units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they reported to me, and I had contact with them as well. This was a brigade that was called the Novo Sarajevo Brigade of Territorial Defence, and when the name Territorial Defence was lost, then it was just called the Novo Sarajevo Brigade, and it remained as part of the defence of the Republic of BH as a whole. Now, as far as I can remember, the commander of the brigade was Mr. Garic. He was a reserve officer from the area itself. They had two battalions, that was their structure, and they explained to me where they were. And the third battalion was on the other side in Pofalici. In other words, behind the Marsal Tito Barracks, on the slopes of the area that gravitates towards Sarajevo. I asked him whether they were able to command that battalion, because there was already an obstacle between them. They had no contact except for radio contact, and they said, Yes, we can maintain contact with them. This battalion later had a disaster met -- a disaster of sorts, not the battalion itself but the people. There was a raid and an incursion of certain forces from Sarajevo and these people were massacred. And that brigade, Garic's brigade, could no longer count on any help from that battalion, but, rather, should rely only on the forces that were on the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Territorial Defence structure that you found when you got there, was it in keeping with the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self Protection or was it a paramilitary force of sorts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As long as it was Territorial Defence, of course, it couldn't be a paramilitary force. It was structured and formed on the basis of the regulation that were in place and they existed as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, how long did you remain in the post of commander of the 1st Romanija Motorised Brigade, and where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of that brigade until the end of 1992, but more accurately, what -- I left the brigade and I happen to recall this by chance, I left on the 4th of February, 1993. I remember that, because that was my birthday. So I left the brigade and handed over the command to the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, and I went to the Drina Corps where I was the Chief of Operations of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you return at any point to Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? If so, when and to what position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's nicely put, when did I return, but please bear with me, but it would be probably better to say I -- it would have been better if I had not returned, but perhaps then you won't take me seriously. Well, I returned toward the end of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to what position were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what positions did you fill?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from early July 1993, I was the Chief of Staff in the corps up until August 1994, more specifically until the 10th of August, when I was appointed corps commander, and I remained in that post through the end of 1995 and early 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I take it that as the second person and then the first man of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as of July 1993 up until the end of war, your adversary was the 1st Sarajevo Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question is good, but it wasn't that I had an adversary. It was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that had on the other side the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's very important for me to point out at this point that these were two armed forces that were well acquainted with one another. I would say they were acquainted in detail. Neither me nor my command or my superiors never -- we never thought or were deluded thinking that the adversary didn't know us, didn't know much about us. Well, in the same manner we knew very well what their strategy would be, what their employment would be, their activities. I would say that we knew it to the last little detail, because this was the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that imply that you also knew the deposition, the deployment of forces, the weapons that they had, the infrastructure? And I'm asking you about the entire 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot command successfully unless you are very familiar with your enemy, and I can confirm here that the deployments, the engagement, the combat fighting, the objectives and intentions, we were very well aware of all of those so that we knew what objectives they had, what intentions they had, and what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you learn these things, or in what manner or manners did you get by information of this nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were several ways. There were a number of ways that we learned about them. The troops -- or, rather, the command, first of all, relies on its intelligence. The collection of data and their analysis would be cross-checked and compared, so one of the sources of information was intelligence. The other manner was this: We were brought to the point where we had to organise an observation system that would confirm the movements and measures and actions taken by the enemy at any particular moment. So there was the observation system or surveillance. The next -- the next manner would be this: On a daily basis, citizens left Sarajevo. They found different ways to accomplish this, and they would provide information to us about what they had seen there and what deployments they had observed, what forces were there, and so on, and of course we had to check this. It is no secret that soldiers informed one another mutually. In other words, from either side, because the lines were very close. They were some 50 metres away, one from the other, so that they communicated amongst themselves, not in terms of providing information, but there were contacts. And the next way, and I think that's probably the most reliable way was that we would assess what the situation was and see what the enemy was employing, what forces, whether they were employing strong forces or weaker forces. So through all these manners, we would -- it would come to the point where we knew everything about our adversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how, in a bit more in detail, how and when you knew the enemy would use stronger or weaker forces? How does ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you're asking me. That's clear to me, but I don't think that was a decisive element. But it was significant, because then we would adapt our own deployments and employment of forces in order to create a situation where we would not be caught by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, on page 11 you said that you were familiar and that you knew the objectives, the intentions that they were trying to accomplish and the purpose of their actions. Could you tell us, first of all, what type of establishment and organisation did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopt, including that of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo? Did that differ in some way? What was the type of organisation and structure that they had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. I have to try to be more precise in my answer in terms of their organisation and formation from the time when they started establishing it at the time when I assumed my post. There was a difference between the early period when they were organised and the second period. Specifically, in 1994, they transitioned to a new type of organisation, new to them. This is not new in the history of the military, but there was this: The command -- brigade commands were attached to the corps command, and that's how this structure functioned. But in the second half of 1994, the 1st Corps of the BH Army transitioned to a new system, the so-called division establishment or system, and specifically they established three divisions. Of the three, one was deployed in Sarajevo. That was the 12th Division of the ground forces. The second one was the 14th Division, which was deployed in the Tarcin sector, which means to the west of Ilidza. And the next division is the 16th Division, whose command was in the Varos sector. This is to the north-west of the theatre in -- vis-a-vis Sarajevo. So there were these three divisions. The corps commander maintains the command in addition to these three divisions that were later structured, and I will explain that in a moment, but he also commanded six independent brigades that were not attached to the divisions. He referred to them as light brigades. Light brigades because they were manoeuvring units. They were not active in combat but were to be used for action along a certain axis. So this was the global structure of the corps. So the command of the corps and its organs, the military police battalion, and the forces that were attached to the corps as a rear structure. Would you like me to describe the structure of the 12th Division? Perhaps I can do that. It's important and topical in view of the fact that these two other divisions were outside of Sarajevo, but this one was deployed in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you use this map to show the Chamber the locations of these division. This is 1D7048 in e-court. Could we please have that map on our screens, and then I'll be asking General Milosevic to use the map to indicate these positions for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7048, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure we can actually see anything on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have nothing showing in e-court. Could you please, sir, use the map on your left-hand side right behind you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we not upload it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the Registry got an error message because it might be too big in its size.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In that case, I would like to ask General Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's uploaded now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's uploaded, but it's still difficult for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you can point out the positions for us on the big map on your left-hand side, and then everybody else can follow on their screens if they like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, do you want the witness to mark on this map or just to explain the general layout?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the general sees the map clearly enough, it would be very good if he could mark for us the contacts or the units of the BH Army that he was actually clashing with, the three divisions first and foremost, and then he can tell us about the meaning of these markings, 3K, 2K, 4K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm getting started. I'll start with positions inside Sarajevo city. As I said, position here fighting actively and engaged here is the 12th Division. The location of Sarajevo city itself, you can see it on this map. I'm not sure if I should mark it at all. It's plain for all to see, Sarajevo, the city itself. The 12th Division --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just put 12D right next to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] All right. That's that position. I know it all too well, if I can put it that way. As for their operations, the operations that they conducted in the actual fighting, well, we'll be showing that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark out the 14th Division of the 1st Corps for us now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not likely, unfortunately. I can't mark the whole sector for you, but I can draw an arrow there to indicate the general direction in which they would operate. I can't quite see it on the map. But here, I'll mark this, although it's for the working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this bit where it says "OG Pazaric"? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not on my map. Oh, right. Okay. It's there. All right. Yes. Operative Group, that's right, near Pazarici, the distance being maybe 5 to 7 kilometres. We have Tarcin. So this is sort of on the Herzegovina side, and that's where the command of the 14th Division was positioned. Its exact combat disposition is something that I can't be very specific about because they held all of this western side of the territory under their control. It's difficult to locate each and every individual unit that belonged to that division, but I can only tell you that they were facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far in the direction of the city centre did they ever get, the 14th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's an excellent question. They covered Igman, Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Butmir, and Kotorac, Donji Kotorac specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, could you tell us as to the provenance of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think General Milosevic could probably tell us about that. We shouldn't move it about too much before it is signed, but perhaps we could explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read on the map itself that it is a working map, but that's all that I have been able to ascertain. I don't know the provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you perhaps check the physical map over there to your left and then see whether you can tell who it belonged to, who it was produced by?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your back, you can take the actual map. Left, to your left, on back side. There. No. Can you see the actual map which is managing on the -- yeah, there. Please look back. You can move, yes. Yes. Do you know what -- the provenance of this map? Could we show the top of the map. It shows Radna Karta or something. Could we unclip the left. Yes. Whose map is this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a war map of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "This is a working map of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it says the 1st of July, 1994. Did I see that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please draw a line, a simple line, connecting the positions of the 14th Division that were closest to you in the city and Pazaric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please erase the previous mark that I left there? It's a very poor mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Fine. So I was trying to draw that arrow before, but that was about something else. It was in this area that the command of the 14th Division was located. This area right here which I'm about to mark is the area covered by the 14th Division along with its 104th Motorised Brigade. So the X that I drew there, the 104th. If you like, I can mark that for you too. 104th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At their forward end, facing you, in other words, could you put an arrow there to mark how far they got in your direction, which is the city itself, and what ground specifically did they cover there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to be very good at drawing things, do I. The area that I marked is about Hrasnica, as far as I can tell. That is the Hrasnica area. But this arrow does not underline the fact sufficiently, because it's showing in exactly the opposite direction. The closest area covered by this brigade is Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, and then down the depth of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was the border between you and them in relation specifically to the location of the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some forces in Butmir and some in Donji Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. No need to worry about your drawing skills. I'd just like to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I have difficulty following this line of evidence. While this is a map that was produced at the time, i.e., July 1994, why do we not see the markings then on this map of 14th Division of 104th Unit, et cetera? Why should we rely on the markings of the general now, and what are these markings then which we see on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm about to ask the general that very same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a working map of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. What about these markings, PRB and so on and so forth? What exactly does that mean? And were the enemy units marked on that map as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a rough disposition and positions of the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and their engagement. Anything that was outside these areas, well, that was the enemy, such enemy forces as actually existed. If we were talking about Ilidza, so we're looking at the Ilidza Infantry Brigade. If we're talking about Hadzici then that would be the Igman Infantry Brigade. If we're look at the area surrounding Rukavica and Trebevic, then that would be the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. If we're talking about area just north of Rajlovac, Vogosca, and all the way up to the eastern side where the Miljacka River meets the city at Sarajevo, that's the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but why don't we have the structure of the 1st Corps based on divisions? On the 4th of July, 1994, were they organised like that already, a division-based structure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right, and that's a good question. They had a brigade-based system back then, not a division-based system. The 1st of July, 1994, no such thing around -- was there. It wasn't before the latter half that they started restructuring. And then the names were new, the numbers were new, and the whole organisational structure was new.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that change anything about the confrontation lines, specifically the forward ends?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're restructuring effort did not affect the combat disposition at all. Well, aside from the fact that the units now had different names and numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I'm looking at Pazaric and Tarcin. Can you mark that as 14D, please, 14D. And then also mark for us the sector covered by the 16th Division.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 16th Division, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't actually see part of it on this map, but ... [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain to the Chamber what this means, 3K and then the number 2 over there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please try to understand me in the right way. It doesn't mean a thing. 3K, that should mean the 3rd Corps. The trouble is it wasn't there at all. So I think it's a mistake that they actually marked this. Right where it says 3K, this was actually covered by the 16th Division and not the 3K that they had in mind. So I stick to my previous remark. I think this is an error in marking. Likewise, here you can see 4K, meaning that on at that side, so from Tarcin onwards in that general direction, which is Mostar, 4K should be the 4th Corps. So you could take that at face value, but what we see around the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps -- I hear some background noise. What you can see about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is the 1st Corps of the BH Army, including the brigades that I specified earlier on. So I'm not talking about the 3rd Corps and the 4th Corps and others. I'm not saying they were actually involved in the fighting. What I'm saying is there was no direct line of contact between them and us at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us about the meaning of that red line just outside the contact zone between 3K and 16D, the red line reaching the lower end of the map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it going through Sarajevo and also beyond. The third line represents the forward end of the defence of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I did not mean the dotted line. I meant the full line there between the number 1 that we see there and --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Essentially that is the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We'll use a small cross to mark that, and then we'll call it "Area of responsibility of the SRK." I have trouble finding my feet in terms of how things are actually marked on this screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 2nd, 3rd, and the 4th Corps that you were not in contact with. Can you please tell us if there was any fighting with those corps and on which occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we had battles with the 2nd Corps throughout the war; in the sense that the 101st Olovo Brigade from the area of Olovo, an inhabited town, that 101st Glorious Brigade, as they called it, was part of the 2nd Corps of the B&H Army, and it was in contact with us in the Nisici sector, the broader area of the Nisici sector, the village of Krivajevici, and so on and so forth. And to be more precise, the Gajne [phoen] village area where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was in contact with the Drina Corps, that's where the initial contact and the conflict with this 101st Brigade began, and that stretched further, our disposition, and now I'm talking about the contact with the 16th Division under the Zvijezda mountain. Then it lay below mount Cemerska, the broader are of the inhabited town of Breza, up to Visoko, and then from Visoko up to Fojnica and then all the way to Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to tell us how long was your forward end on the outside edge with the enemy and how long was it in the inner perimeter around the city centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the city centre. This is what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. You are correct. But can you please tell us how long the contact -- the line of contact was between you and the 12th Division.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes these estimates are not precise. However, using the instruments that we had to measure this length, we calculated that it was somewhere in the area of 50 kilometres. The total area of our forward defence and was 240 kilometres from the north, north-east to be more precise, from the north-east through these areas that I mentioned below mount Zvijezda and then Visoko up to mount Treskavica is 250 kilometres; or, if I were to use different parameters, from -- then from the extreme right left wing [as interpreted] of the corps to the extreme left wing, I would need 250 kilometres length along the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Based on this map, can you also tell us which area on the map could be considered to be an area where there was no front, no firing, to be an area where life was normal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no area there without fierce fighting. Of course, the intensity of the fighting centred on Sarajevo, mutual fighting, but there were situations, very difficult ones at that, when the intensity of fighting would increase precisely from the sectors of the 16th and the 14th Division, and of course in strict joint action with the 12th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Could I please ask you to put your initials and the date in the lower right-hand corner. And I would like to draw everybody's attention to P842. This is a map, a Prosecution document that perhaps demonstrates the structure of the divisions in the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to put the date here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the lower right-hand corner. Could you please put your -- date and have no concerns about your handwriting. We are all aware that you did lose an eye in the war.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, thank you very much. I would like to tender the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly turn back and read the legend for us, which is on the left bottom of the map. You can see it on the actual map. Could you read out for us the three lines.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first line, "Line of contact." Second line says "Line of contact as of the 3rd of August, 1994." And the third line states "Line of contact as of the 24th of May, 1994." Actually, no, I apologise. The 24th of August, the 24th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit this marked map as well as the unmarked map. Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, and Dr. Karadzic was quite right. P842, if part of the point of this was to illustrate the division structure, is the map that is the witness's own map that sets that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The unannotated map which is 65 ter 1D7048 will be Exhibit D2788, and the annotated version will be Exhibit D2789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need to look at the map any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir. Can you help us with this: Can we take a look at the forces that were later part of the 12th Division? These were forces that were in Sarajevo itself. What was the strength of that force? I'm going to try to put my questions in such a way that you can give me short answers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, would I kindly ask, but I will also try to be rational and try to give short answers, but you don't get good information in short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you please just go ahead and say as much as you need to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. Thank you. Could you please put your question again? I didn't understand the point of it properly. I didn't understand the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, never mind. In the town itself, the forces that later made up the 12th Division, could you please tell us what the structure was, what the forces were that made up the division? What were you faced with from the city in terms of forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is why I asked you to repeat the question, because it's not only the 12th Division that's involved. It would be insufficient just to discuss the structure of the 12th Division. Right from the start, what I want to say is that besides the 12th Division, there was also action by other forces that I will mention later. The 12th Division, under the command of Colonel Prevljak - I've forgotten his first name for the moment - it comprised eight brigades, eight mountain brigades. There were changes there. Some were renamed to motorised brigades later, then mountain brigades, but in essence the point is that there were eight brigades. These were strong units, very uniformly deployed, and I can add that I was quite amazed at their military skill in deploying the defence and also the way those forces were used. Not just the defence. It was under the command of Fikret Prevljak, that's right. That was the 101st Mountain Brigade. That 101st Mountain Brigade was one of the most or one the strongest units in this particular set-up, and it was under the command of Colonel Fikret Hodzic, an officer who belonged to the category of smart people. I know him, and I know all the others as well. Then the next unit, I don't have to go by the actual sectors, but they all focused on Mojmilo, Grbavica, up to the Vrbanja Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you also give us the sector roughly, the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the area, Mojmilo Hill, which dominates Lukavica. It covers the territory and protects in the form of a geographical topographical feature that is 3.5 kilometres long at an elevation of 620-something metres above sea level, and that area was where the 101st Mountain Brigade was deployed, and this brigade stretched across Ozrenska Street, in the Zeljeznicar stadium sector. Then it reached the Miljacka River all the way to the Vrbanja Bridge up to Marin Dvor to be precise. It had its area and the depth that it was covering, and it was covering all the neighbourhoods that were behind its back: Otokaz [phoen], Rakeno Selo [phoen] and the annex Cengic Vila 1 and so on and so forth. Then from the Vrbanja Bridge was where the 115th Brigade was deployed. It's a famous brigade known to all because it was under the command of the infamous Caco, whom they then liquidated in an action. That's the 115th Brigade. It's area of responsibility begins from Vrbanja Bridge, and then it stretches above Vraca up to Debelo Brdo hill. From Debelo Brdo it is deployed towards the so-called Colina Kapa. From Colina Kapa, the area then continues to the east to the Miljacka River where the Miljacka River enters Sarajevo, and that's where its forward end begins. And its depth is up to the centre of town itself, including Skenderija, Sirokaca, Bistrik, that whole area of the city with its line of decisive defence and launching attacks at us. From there that brigade demonstrated a lot of extreme conduct. I know the commander. They probably inherited their aggressive stance from a previous period and so on and so forth. Then the 152nd Brigade takes over which covers that area from the Miljacka River towards the Hladivode sector. That's its forward end. And its depth stretches all the way to the city hall, the famous city hall in Sarajevo. Actually it's the Bascarsija area. That's that sector. The commander of that brigade belonged to the category of people who knew how to carry out the command duties, and he demonstrated a normal attitude, one that can be given respect and was chivalrous. Then this is the 105th Brigade that was in charge of the Jajce barracks in that area. Then the 105th Mountain Brigade takes over which was a brigade with seven battalions. It's a very large powerful unit. I cannot recall the name of the commander right now, but I do know it well. He had seven battalions, and out of those seven, four were infantry battalions. There was one Engineers Battalion, an artillery division and then one was a Logistics Unit. The brigade held the area of Sedrenik, everything above the Kosevo Hospital, the Breka area, and it linked up to the 152nd Brigade, and its depth lay all the way back to the railway station, and it held the centre of the city. The brigade was stronger than a third of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It was very strong. It was very well equipped, had good combat equipment, powerful equipment and I would say that not everything was quite proper in their relationship and in these conflicts and in the fighting. They didn't fire in a normal manner but in a manner which would turn into an attempt to destroy us. And they tried to do that. So then Hladivode towards Orahov Brijeg hill. That's where their area was. The same brigade went over Prevoj, the Grdonj peak, and it joined up through Pionirska Dolina valley with the 111th. The 111th would sometimes be called a Mountain Brigade and sometimes a Motorised Brigade. The 111th, its forward disposition spread from that geographical feature, Orahov Brijeg, through the faculty for transport which is now in Vogosca, to the elevations, the so-called Krcevine elevations, and it covered the highest elevations in Sarajevo, above the town of Sarajevo; and that is Orlic, 840 metres, then Zuc, then Vis, all of them all the way to the area above Rajlovac. And it dominated Vogosca. It could see it really well. It was an inhabited settlement. It was impossible to move around in Vogosca because of the very strong shelling. Perhaps there was some obstacles or barriers put up. Some railway carriages from the railway carriage factory were put up so that people could move. If you permit me, that area was so exposed to fire that it was impossible, unbearable to live there but people managed somehow. Then that linked up to the 112th Brigade, which from that place, from the 111th Brigade, took over the area all the way to the place where the Miljacka River leaves Sarajevo. Miljacka enters Sarajevo on the eastern side. It leaves it on the western side, and that is where the area covered by the 112th Division ended. That division -- actually, not division, that brigade, had a powerful artillery component. These were key positions, artillery firing positions, which they fired from with the weapons that they had at their disposal. From the 112th, the -- and let me add that the 112th and the 111th also covered in the depth the area all the way to Dzemala Bijedica [phoen] Street. Then follows 102nd Mountain Brigade. That was one of the more agile brigades, because they were constantly engaged in combat and in trying to destroy the area of Nedzarici. That was their idea, or whatever, and over that area to link up with the 104th that I mentioned earlier. Now, the 102nd Brigade held or covered the area from the Miljacka bridge over the Stup hill, along the student halls, and there it would cross into Nedzarici. On -- onward from it was the 155th Brigade, Mountain Brigade, under the command of Ismet Hadzic, who was a civilian. The 155th Brigade was in Dobrinja, and in my view it was a unit that was very numerous, the personnel, and they were in a very small area, so they were getting out of control. So I understood that they needed more space to try to break through. So they opened fire on Lukavica and Trapare neighbourhood, as well as some houses on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like to call up 1D7047 in e-court. You will be familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in line 1 on the 30th page, the general didn't say that they were out of control. He said that they were acting in a very wild manner. They were uncontrolled. They were aggressive. Now, could I request that the usher provide a printout of the document that we've called in e-court, 1D7047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not uploaded in e-court? I don't see it on the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, who drafted this map -- or, rather, this disposition of units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did. Observing the situation, revealing their disposition and deployments and observing their direction of action, I managed to put together a mosaic of their activities, and right now looking at it, I'm not quite happy because you cannot really see clearly the extent to which they engaged in combat and opened fire. You can't really see it from this map, but it gives you an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about the brigades and their dispositions. Can that be seen on this map? You started with the 101st, moved eastward all the way to 155th to the west.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I tried to present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do have a printout of the map that you can look at.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You see, the semicircles there, the arcs -- maybe I can show it here. For instance, here. This marks the place where these units had contact, physical contact. Likewise, right here, that's where they linked up. You can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which units were adjacent above Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the point contact between 105th and 112th -- no, 111th. No, 112th. My apology. So the 112th and the 105th, which spread from Sedrenik via Grdonj to Orahov Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will -- we're approaching the time for our break, so would you please date and sign this map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. This is okay. I've checked again. It's okay. So I should put the date there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the date and your signature, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid today is the 23rd, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction. I need to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the general is putting the date, probably we need the translation of each legend later on. So we'll mark this map for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. Karadzic. Shall we take a break if it is convenient?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you have a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A very quick point, Mr. President. The witness wanted to address the Trial Chamber in respect of his detention conditions very quickly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have to turn to Mr. Robinson and Mr. Bourgon whether we can stay in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Actually, he just wants to say that he's satisfied and say thank you to the Trial Chamber, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me this opportunity to say this. Perhaps I should have asked for this myself, but very well. I need to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me to have, while in detention, the conditions that are similar to the ones that I have in the prison in (redacted). In other words, I'm not isolated from the other prisoners. And let me just add one thing. Yesterday when I was asked about the notes that I had jotted down, it was only then that I concluded that I was happy that I had already jotted down some of my notes while I was still in (redacted) in Estonia, because when I arrived here and under the conditions that I originally had, I wouldn't have been able to concentrate, but right now everything is fine, and thank you very much. I'm quite happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the court deputy approach the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll a break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would now like to show you a document from the command of the 12th Division of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up, please, in e-court 1D2839.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, first of all, could you tell us what the handwritten note means, and could you tell us who wrote that? Could you read it out to us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is my own handwritten note when I tried to communicate with my attorney and show him a source document, an original document, which shows the exact deployment and shows accurately the engagement of the 12th Division forces, and the intention was for him to understand the problems and to gain insight into this from this document, to gain insight into the adversary or the other side for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And this request of mine was something he did not like. I can't explain why, but he just couldn't understand it, and he did not want to tender this document, and this document was never used in trial -- in my trial. So this is my answer to your question, to explain what happened with this document and my request to use it. But if you need anything else, please just let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what -- first of all, tell us what kind of document is this? This is an order. What kind of order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order for decisive defence by the commander of the 12th Division, dated the 14th of April, 1995. The gist of the document is this: He expresses here the deployment of his forces, and he gives a detailed account of everything that his commanders need to know, including what assets they have at their disposal, what resources, what area of responsibility they're responsible for and the direction or the axis, the axis of their advance and attacks, although here it says this is a command for a decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what it says in the third line of this text. What was his estimate of the forces that he had against him, the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He states here that that's 9.000 troops, yes. He wasn't far off the mark. I believe that his estimate was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the other 9.000 troops of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Where were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The remainder or the other part of the corps -- although let's be clear on this, both these men and the other men, they're all part of one and the same corps. They were deployed at the wider area at the Nisici plateau, Nisiskavi Soravan [phoen], and including all the areas that were tied up to Visoko and Olovo and Breza. Now, the other elements of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were deployed in the general area in the southern front below Treskavica; in other words, in the Trnovo settlement area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that it's very difficult to follow this line of questioning without having an English translation. And I find it also difficult to understand why we do not have English translation of this document while it was put to one of the witnesses, i.e., Martin Bell, about two years ago, one and a half years ago. Two years ago, more than two years ago, according to what e-court says to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have requested a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you put in a request for translation, Mr. Karadzic? I think the e-court says it was put to Martin Bell on 15th of December, 2010.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we always have to prioritise, and it is possible that we've overlooked this document as one of the priority documents, but I do believe that we have made a request for its translation, and of course there is a logjam in the translation service, so we do understand that they don't have time to meet the dead-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it at that. Mr. Milosevic, could you kindly read out your handwriting for us to understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank God. Your Honour, it says here, that's what I wrote in my own hand -- well, first of all what you see there which is kind of pale, that says "Important." That meant that it was an important document, as far as I was concerned. Now, what it reads here in handwriting is: "We should finally resolve with the attorney the issue about the presentation on a map of a developed deployment of the 12th Division in the town of Sarajevo. Decidedly developed deployment of the 12th Division in the town of Sarajevo." In other words, I asked him to translate this onto a map so that we can see from the map where that was, but he never did any of those things that I asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I also find it difficult if your attorney did not tender this document, how could this document be in the custody of Mr. Karadzic? Do you have any clue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour -- your Excellency, that this is somewhere --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. All I know is that this was what I asked my attorney to do, my Defence counsel. This document was important, as I've already said, in my view. Now, whether this was transposed, I actually had the same suggestion for the trial of Mr. -- the Chief of the General Staff who was also connected to this, yes, Perisic, for the Perisic case. And perhaps in that form it actually appeared somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will look at the bottom of the page, because perhaps the document was marked for identification. Further down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. We have a number there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, line 3, what was the estimate of troops facing the 12th Division, overall strength?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine thousand men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Page 2, please, paragraph 4. It starts with the words "I hereby decide." What about the structure of their decisions? Are they similar to the your decisions, because I noticed in VRS documents that paragraph 4 is always "I hereby decide."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite true, but let me just add one thing. We all come from the same military background. Officers on both sides were trained in much the same way, and the same applied to procedures based on which orders and reports were written up. So the command methods were very much alike on both sides of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please focus on 5.1. What is the brigade that he is talking about there? We shall not be dwelling on this, but what is that brigade, and how does he identify their position, and is that consistent with your information at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 101st Brigade minus one battalion. This sort of indication minus one, you'll find that elsewhere, too, because they'll always have one battalion from a brigade and then send it out elsewhere, send it to Niksic, for example, that area over there. So we're looking at the 101st Brigade and what I see here is consistent with the disposition that I was aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be MFI'd. We have a similar document that we do have a translation for that again gives you the deployment of units belonging to the 12th Division two months later. It is an attack plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Chamber something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be a good idea to focus on this part where it talks about the combat disposition. The fact reflected here shows the force and equipment available to the commander of the 12th Division. He states in unambiguous terms that he has some forces in one of the echelons with some reservists and that there were some support forces available too. So support was available. And the other commander knew that he could lend support if he needed. So he had artillery. He had the anti-armour, he had anti-aircraft, he had some obstacles available to him, and he has the appropriate command forces available to him; in one word, he has everything that he needs to effectively run the forces available to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I was moving to -- to have this MFI'd, and then perhaps we could sum up in e-court a very similar document that we do have a translation for and all the same elements are actually there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for the record, I was told that the number we saw at the bottom of page 1 is a Defence identification number, not anything else. Yes. Ms. Edgerton, do you have any objection to marking this document for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For identification, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D2791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 1D2567.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is an attack order. What is the date, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attack order by the commander of the 12th Division, 11th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this attack carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is no ordinary attack. This is an offensive. The scope of this offensive is brought, the scope of the operations is brought. This operation was meant to crush the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 1, line 3. This is two months later. What is the estimate of -- of the men he was facing, the number of men he was facing now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's down to 8.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the estimate was actually correct, because many of my men had been killed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does he say there about the 12th Division and the neighbouring divisions, the 14th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without reading I know the context, and I know what you're asking me. There was a full co-ordination of combat operations between both of these units. It's a very clever way to co-ordinate your operations from Sarajevo on the one hand - when I say clever, I mean clever for their own purposes, of course - and combining that with the forces outside Sarajevo but moving in on Sarajevo. The 12th Division was in Sarajevo, and the 14th and 16th Divisions from the area that I specified. Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have the next page in English, please. Please continue, General, sir. Tell us briefly about what -- what this is about. What force, are available to him and what exactly does he intend to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the commander of the 12th Division?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. What does the document tell us about his intentions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document tells us that all of his forces were active by this time. A while ago we were talking about him co-ordinating with the 14th and the 16th Divisions. In actual fact, it was the corps commander who was doing the co-ordination for him, but he knows that co-ordination will be there, that there will be concerted action. He knows with sure and certain knowledge that heading his way are these other units, but not just from the 1st Corps in relation to this specific situation, and it's not he who is saying this, it's the corps commander telling him what other forces would be involved. The 3rd Corps under General Mahmuljin's command, the 7th Corps, another powerful unit in his own area. The 4th Corps under elements of the 2nd Corps. So all these units together along with the 1st Corps were the strike force threatening the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So they're calling this -- they're labelling this as deblocking [Realtime transcript read in error "disabling"] Sarajevo. I don't mind that, because that's what it was from their perspective, I suppose. So that certainly was not a deblocking effort. This was about crushing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down to the bottom of the English page where it starts to talk about forces and combat disposition. And that is the next page in the Serbian copy, so you can tell us about what it means, combat disposition. Can we have the next page in both versions of the document, please. Can we zoom in, please. We need page number 3 in the Serbian. Page number 3 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly about what the decision comprises and then what forces would actually be used.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of this decision. First of all, he decides to hold on to what he has already, use some of his forces to secure the defence line, and also to use some other units available to him to carry out certain operations and to achieve certain breakthroughs in certain areas. I don't know this by heart, but I know the general direction in which they were moving. Talking of the 12th Division, it was launching operations, trying to break out of Sarajevo using its own brigades along its own axes of operations. Talking about the combat disposition of these forces here, what you see here constitutes a corroboration. He wanted to do this, and he was indeed able to do this. He was able to launch this operation. When a commander decides to lend support to someone, then the other person has to be aware of the fact that there is support coming his way, support in terms of firing, in terms of firepower, support in terms of reinforcements being sent his way. This person must know that he will not be left to his own devices, but help is coming. So these are not particularly adventurous or risky decisions. These are well-thought-out decisions and they are at this point in time ready to go ahead with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us about the combat disposition and the units that were available to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- before you answer, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting but just before it appears on our screen at page 41, line 5, we see the word "disabling Sarajevo" used and I distinctly heard the witness say "deblocking Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go on further, Mr. Milosevic, could you read the handwritten part at the bottom of paragraph 5.1, and tell us whether it is written in Cyrillic or in Latin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uh-huh. If this is what you're asking me about -- it's gone now. Latin script it is. Yes. It's a clarification that I jotted down myself, because this is my handwriting. It's about this abbreviation, DAG-12, the division artillery group. I did this because I knew that my Defence counsel understood nothing about these abbreviations and he couldn't possibly figure out what it meant. So I would expand these for his benefit in a bid to explain to him what he was going through. So this is the division artillery group belonging to the 12th Division in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this page, but can we see the first page, page 1 of this document in B/C/S. So, Mr. Karadzic, this document is from Mr. Milosevic's case. Exhibit D417 is from his case? And, Mr. Milosevic, I see "Plan B" in Cyrillic in the middle of -- on top of the page in Cyrillic. Do you read -- do you see that, "Plan B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it your handwriting, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't. I don't know whose it is. I don't write in Cyrillic. I think this is probably written by my Defence counsel, "Plan T." So linking up the code-name of the entire operation, Tekbir. The 1st Corps, the BH Army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question for you was whether you could tell us about the combat disposition and the units that were available to this commander. That is the question from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could we please go back to that portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 3 in the Serbian. Combat disposition and then the units.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to embark on that. The commander here decides to keep some attacking forces, some of the units involved. And to also use some of the units to defend and to offer support, some of the units to be involved in anti-armoured combat. Artillery support, that is understood. When he says support, it's not about actually fetching them a glass of water. Of course, it's about offering support in terms of the firepower, anti-aircraft, and then also some forces to secure the actual combat operations, and that is an element, the importance of which cannot be overestimated. Very important. Signals and command and also reserve. We see everything that is available to him, and he has all of the required elements assembled him there, leaving him in an almost ideal position to carry out combat operations. He has everything that he needs in order to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What about 5.1, 5.2? What are the forces there that he's using? Where are these forces positioned, and what about the command posts and forward command posts? Where are those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When discussing these forces that he engaged, first of all, he engaged all of the forces at their disposal, the brigades that I mentioned previously. These are the brigades from the 12th Division. What you can see here, that the independent brigades are also taking part, which are directly in line of command under the corps. These are light brigades. The list of documents with the commanders receiving the order, other than his commanders from the 101st, 102nd, 115th, and so on and so forth, there is also the signature of the commander of the police forces brigade, Mr. Mirkovic. And this is an additional unit outside of the MUP B and H special brigade. It was called the Bosna Brigade. This brigade is purely a police brigade. They had an excess of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us this entire paragraph 5.1 about the 112th Brigade? Can you tell us, General, sir, when you lost your right eye?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost my eye in 1995 at Bosut.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please enlarge this for the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you lose your eye?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a direct hit by a tank shell at the observation post of the commander, my observation post. It hit directly the observation post. I wasn't hit myself directly, but I did lose my right eye in this hit. The fire originated from Sarajevo, from the Velesici incline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this, and then for the others could you please tell us what is supported and what the command forces are? Could you read 5.1, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 112th Viteska Mountain Brigade in decisive defence defends the area of responsibility of the brigade while a part of the forces from the forward section Vis Lemezi is to carry out an attack along the axis of Vis, Perivoj, trig point K 6.34, Dvor and Mijatovici, Mijatovici Kosa, Zabrdje with the objective as follows: By energetic action of the forces from the front route the enemy along the axis of attack, inflict as many losses as possible in manpower and materiel, capture the facilities at Perivoj, elevation 6.34, Mijatovici Strana, trig point 5.82, the village of Mijatovici, the village of Zabrdje, and break out to the Rajlovac-Semizovac road, and in close joint action with the 111th Light Brigade and the 143rd Light Brigade organise a defence, repulse a possible attack, and be prepared to link up with the forces of the 7th Corps. And the 7th corps would then proceed from that direction towards Reljevo from the direction of Visoko.
