utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the translation on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, your last question and answer were not reflected in the transcript because you overlapped with the interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you able to tell us as it refers to 5.1, who supports? What does that imply? Where's the command post, and where's the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all right. I understood it now. I thought you meant the overall support for the entire 12th Division. All right. So as far as this brigade is concerned you noticed that well. This brigade is being supported by the 12th Division Artillery Group. The command post of this brigade is in -- at Astra. Astra is right in the middle of town. And the forward command post is in the sector of Sokolje, and that Sokolje dominates Rajlovac, and throughout the war Rajlovac was under the same pressure as Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now scroll up where it says this part is -- supports also the 146th Light -- not to scroll down but to scroll up. [In English] All the way down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is discussed here is the support provided to the 143rd Light Brigade. They are supported by the artillery group of the division, the command post would be in the sector of the Ramiz Slacin barracks. That used to be my barracks, Victor Bubanj. And its command post, the command post of this brigade pursuant to the decision of the brigade commander, I mean the commander picks his own command post, the command post of the 143rd Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And all of this, is that in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I will wait. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have English translation for this. There is no point of asking the witness to read out whole paragraphs. Of course, it is for you to use your time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not entire paragraphs, your Excellency. I just wanted him to identify the support and the command post for each brigade and to tell us where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. General, can you please tell us where the 111th -- actually, just these three paragraphs. Just these three lines at the end of the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I can see the 111th at the top of the page. It's being supported by the artillery group 12, the command is in the sector of the Blagoje Parovic school. The forward command post is in the Orlic sector. It's a trig point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to try in order to get things to move faster, let's look at a hundred -- the 105th. Let's skip the MUP forces paragraph. 105th. Does it not state here it's supported by the division's artillery group? The command post is in the sector of the park, and the forward command post is in the sector of the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it states here is what it is, and the fact that the command post is in the park sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think that's the best way to move forward in phrasing your question. Dr. Karadzic has led the witness a few times now, and as we get into the documents particularly, perhaps he could be cautioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it has been the practice of the Chamber to allow the accused to put leading questions until objected to by the Prosecution, and unless it is a serious problem, we'll let him continue. Please bear in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will just ask the General then where the forward command post was supposed to be for the 105th Brigade, the command post and the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently the forward command post -- the commander, this commander, was obviously told that he could legally place his command post at the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the next command, where would the command post be? General, sir, is all of this within the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is a neighbourhood when we're talking about the forward command post, and if we're talking about the 152nd Brigade, this area of Vratnik, this is a neighbourhood above Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll up, please, so we can see the bottom of the page. What about this 115th? What is this 6th April square, and what is Mala Kula?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The 6th April square, that's the area where the command of the 2nd Military District was, and it's a -- actually, it's in the very centre of town, Bistrik. The forward command post is in Mala Kula. I really cannot tell you what this place is. There was a number of "kulas," towers, around Sarajevo, so I don't know exactly which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at the following page, so that we can see -- we will not be looking at the other ones because there is a translation. And then where it says firing support, what is this firing support and what do they have at their disposal in the town itself? Let's look at the page in B/C/S, and the participants can look for themselves for the English version. Can we look at the bottom of the page, item 6.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in a little bit on the text? Ah, all right. Thank you. I don't know if I should read this. The fire support is provided by the division of the artillery group which is part of the 3rd Battery of the 2nd MAP. There's an anti-air -- a rocket battery. The commander of the 3rd MAD, all the weaponry from the 3rd MAD are to be deployed at the basic firing positions in the sectors of Hum, Busca, Mojmilo, Zrak, Orlovaca. The main observation posts in the sectors of Hum, Orlic, Svabino Brdo, Mojmilo Brdo, the command post of the 12th DAG is in the sector of Velesici and the forward command post is in the sector of Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. I would like to tender this document. I don't need to go any further and read the document because the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you saw the command post, the forward command posts, and then you said that all of them were located in the city itself. I wanted to ask you what a command post of a force consists of. What are the elements, where are they deployed, and what kind of an area do they occupy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know that the general has said that he saw the command posts and saw the forward command posts, as Dr. Karadzic has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the general said, not that he saw. He said that he read from the document that these command posts were at localities that he indicated as being within the city areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. Can you please tell us, all those command posts and all of that that refer to the 12th Division, all of that, was that in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just allow me to clarify that a little bit, the question of that structure, the command structure. That is a key structure for the -- for any combat unit. No one can act in any way if they don't have a command that would provide guidance. And may I add, with the indulgence of the Trial Chamber, when my lawyer -- actually, he just talked about the number of people. There are 50.000 people in Sarajevo, 50.000 people in Sarajevo, and so on and so forth, and I said that that was not sufficient, because if the people are disorganised and there's no command, then it's just a mob and nothing else. We're talking about organised structures here with a command structure that is developed, and this is what is significant. It is correct that these command posts were located in the city. When it says in the park, in the park that is in the Trapare Street, and that is a street and an area that I am familiar with. I know where it is located. It's in the centre of the city. Specifically, the command of the 12th Division was located in the Skenderija sector and the brigade commands practically in the same way had their own command posts just like the corps command did in the centre of town. All of them were in the centre of town. If we're talking about command posts, these are elements that have their complete infrastructure, I would say, which has to do with the system of communications, the system of security, system of parking, and system of processing and preparation of food in order to feed the cadre, to issue tasks, for holding meetings, to also have the functioning messenger and courier service so that in the existing command posts which function in Sarajevo, there is a very lively activity going on constantly which was observable. When madam said that I did not see that, it's not me, but using our observation system, we could all observe that. You could see all of this, and then when you look at these documents, you can see that all of that was correct. I don't know if I was clear enough, that when you talk about the system of command posts and the distribution of command posts, that it's not just one point where a person is sitting and issuing orders. That is where everything originates from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1D7202, and can I ask you to explain to us what this document is and what these markings are and who drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. What I would like to stress here is that I drew this myself in an attempt to just give you an idea what -- how these things work. So this is not any particular command post. This is really just a concept, a depiction of the deployment of forces at a command post. So on the right-hand side where we see the communications system or signals system, there are certain command organs that are connected, interconnected, within this entire system. In other words, via the Chief of Staff, they all are connected to the commander. All organs of a certain command have to be there represented, including the operations organ, and they're in charge of monitoring the entire situation, giving proposals and guidelines. Then there's the security organ, and attached to these two, the operations and the Chief of Staff organs, we have the various arms, infantry, artillery, and other arms that would be part of their complement of a certain -- of any given unit. The system of technical and radar support is also depicted here, and this is in fact the key service. All the other elements are just auxiliary elements such as security units, military police units, and very close to them are the reconnaissance companies, depending on the unit, because not every unit would have a reconnaissance company. Then there is also the area for the military police, and we see the location where food is prepared as well as supplies for the organs that are in that area that operate there. And we also see support services or support resources for fire purposes in the event that this command post would be discovered and that somebody opened fire on them. So this would be a battery, an elaborate battery for the protection of the command post.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the usher please assist the general with the pen so that he can mark this on his drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us where it says at the bottom an elaborate or developed command post? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it means. It means that this is a depiction of an elaborate developed command post with all the services that are within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what the designation there which says "Staff Command" or "Headquarters Staff"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are the assisting organs that assist with logistics, that provide logistics for a system like this. For instance, a brigade would have its logistics department; so does a command post. It has to have its own logistics, and it is called staff -- headquarters staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put a number 2 where it says IC or Ech. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the reconnaissance company. That's all it could mean, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other marking there where it says "Potential force -- intervention forces," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each command post has to have a unit nearby that is to be employed for interventions. Now, how large that unit should be, the intervention unit, that would depend on the circumstances. If the commander feels that he should have an intervention unit, then he would establish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put the number 3 next to the possible intervention force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a number 4 next to "CVP" or "CVP" and tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the Military Police Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you put a number 5 next to the parking area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably a universal international signal for parking. Well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is "Pija"? There is something there which reads P-i-j-a. What is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the reception area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us there at the top what that is and mark it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll put number 7 here, and that's the artillery battery. It's a support unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Support -- in support of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the event that the command post is discovered and is targeted, if the sector of the command post is targeted, then there must be a support unit that would be used to neutralise the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you move to the right and tell us what this image, the tripod there, what is that? What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the radar, so I'll put an R next to number 8. I apologise. In fact -- my apologies. I really am sorry. It's my fault. This is a radio relay device, in fact, a radio relay device which assists in maintaining communications with the brigades. The commander has communication with brigades and subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does this CV stand for? CV, communications centre.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what it means, the signals centre or communications centre. Here's number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what this POM stands for, POM and then Moral, M-o-r-a-l. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the assistant for morale. Well, this is the heart of the command. The command -- the commander has everything tied to him. So he has the assistant for morale, an assistant for intelligence, and also an entire structure at his disposal to enable him to monitor the operation that he's in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you don't have to go -- we don't have to go any further -- into any further detail here. It will be translated. But can you tell me what this flag represents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each command has its own flag. So this would represent schematically the command post of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you put a number 10 next to it, and could you tell us what the marking for a brigade or a battalion would be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could show you if you give me a piece of paper so I could draw on it -- or maybe I can try doing it here. So this type of flag would indicate a battalion, a command post of a battalion, because you have to make a distinction, because not all commands are of the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please put a number 11 next to it, and please date and sign this drawing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So it's the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, would you agree that we need a translation of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm actually not sure how my colleagues who are very qualified will be able to deal with the very slim abbreviations and acronyms. It might be more useful if the general explains them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The remainder that he hasn't explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you start with the security, Mr. Milosevic, OB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. OB stands for security and intelligence, a security and intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, let me just explain. This can only be -- this can be either an intelligence organ or an intelligence plus security organ, both. They could both be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twelve, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already have an 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct, 12. And 13 for the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirteen for the commander. Here it is. His vehicle is there, and he's always ready to be on the move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 14 for Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does OC mean, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Operations Centre. It's a room where operations officers sit and work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you need more explanation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do we need to -- I don't think so. We'll admit this marked diagram, but I will mark it for identification pending -- I don't think we need translation at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Now I think it's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you now tell us how many of these elaborate staffs or headquarters of units were there in total in Sarajevo as part of what was later to be called the 12th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the 12th Division and its subordinate units, there were other command posts as well there, so that the number of command posts in Sarajevo were not solely restricted to the 12th Division, and I'll explain that in a moment. This division had three command posts of its own, the basic command post; the rear command post, that's a separate post; and the forward command post. So these are the division command posts alone. Now, the 1st Corps had the same structure, the same, the same system. Of course it was a larger command, but there was a larger number of personnel there. There was the basic command post, the forward command post, and the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said Danijela Ozme, at Danijela Ozme. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the Danijela Ozme Street. That's where the basic command post was. And this is the area that they claim had never been hit by anything, and of course no one would even attempt to target it, because that was the centre of town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to these, I represented in a different form -- I've explained that the division numbers eight brigades, these mountain brigades, and each of these brigades has a similar command post as the one depicted, but perhaps with a fewer number of men. They would all have these three different posts. Now, the next thing is this: Within Sarajevo itself, there were two brigades which were located in Sarajevo itself, but they were not attached to this division but, rather, to the 1st Corps. Now, these eight brigades, separate from the ninth that I mentioned that belonged to the 14th Division which was the 104th Brigade in Hrasnica. Brigades have their own battalions, and the total number of battalion command posts, and I stress these are smaller sites with a fewer number of men. There were 55 of them in total in Sarajevo. Now, each of those battalions has a company. Some have three companies, some have four. But if we add all that up, the total number of command posts including the battalion companies and the independent companies that belong to the 12th Division or, for instance, the Military Police Company, the reconnaissance, sabotage company and so on and so forth, they all existed, and their command posts that are placed by the company commander with his own structures, there were 164 of those. I have written all this down. I'm not sure if I've added up this correctly, if I did the calculation right, but I believe that in total there were 200 or so command posts in total there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Trial Chamber allow the witness to look at his notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary. I don't understand any problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] The number of command posts was 275. These were command posts for the units that I've already mentioned, the command posts that existed within the brigades and divisions, but I failed to mention that there is another structure there, a police command structure. This was the special MUP Brigade. So in addition to the others, there were eight other command posts that were command posts at Ilidza, at Pale, Vogosca -- not command posts but commands, commands that commanded forces. They were in all these municipalities that were on the outskirts of Sarajevo. These were military commands that existed in Sarajevo and had their own structure, but of course these were smaller. So that's how they increased these numbers. And they were working on preparing the forces that would break out of Sarajevo so that they could continue commanding those units when they entered, for instance, Rajlovac, Pale, Ilidza, and so on and so forth. So from this we can see that they had -- that their intention was offensive and the area that they called, they would use the term "temporarily captured territory," which is a category that existed in the one-time JNA strategy of combat, and it referred to situations where NATO would carry out an aggression against Yugoslavia or the Warsaw Pact so that then each area, had it been captured, would have been referred as to temporarily captured. Now, from this fact -- or on this fact they built this structure, and the families that had lived there for ages, they were treated as civilians being in captured territories, and they wanted to expel them from those areas. So I am just trying to say that there were these command posts. They were visible. They functioned. They commanded and directed their forces, and in the end there was fighting against those forces with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. What about the 275 plus 8 for all these peripheral municipalities. What about all these command posts, the 275? Does that imply a single location or could a single command post occupy a number of different locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is perfectly clear. There are some levels that have command posts in three different versions, the basic command post, the rear command post, and the forward command post. But a platoon or a company wouldn't have that. A company would not have a rear command post. A company commander would have his own station, then a station for his combat needs. He would have several assistants. He would have messengers and so on and so forth. They would only be in a single location, the company would, because that is a lower level so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about larger units, a command post in a single location or perhaps in several different locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would be three locations, as I said, in order to be able to operate. That is the first thing. Secondly, they wouldn't even need to be in a single location, strictly speaking. There would be some distance between the various sections of the command. Just to name an example, the 104th Brigade, for example, has a part of its command in Butmir, and the 104th Brigade is the brigade that we're talking about. It operates and exists in the Hrasnica area. So a part of it is there. And then if I may just clarify now that I've been given an opportunity. In the Butmir area and the Sokolovic Kruna area, you can also find a part of the corps command. I didn't indicate their existence here as a separate component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us where the Supreme Command of the BH Army was located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I don't know. It is known that the Presidency occupied the Presidency building. I'm not sure if they saw the same building also as their Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about elements of the Main Staff of the BH Army within the city itself, because that's what we're talking about, the city itself.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. The part of the General Staff command, the part, and that is why they had some men there for their own security, the Guards Brigade, a unit that we have not mentioned so far, although it was there in addition to all the brigades that I have so far enumerated. So a part of the General Staff command was indeed in Sarajevo in a number of different locations, as a matter of fact. And I can't say for sure what those locations were. The remainder, and the principal component of the command was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the 1st Corps command? Was it in the city itself or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Corps command, as I said, was at Danijela Ozme Street near the main hygiene office. There's a big park in the middle of Sarajevo, just across the street from the Presidency building. It's difficult to keep track, because I have forgotten a lot of the streets involved, although I did live there at one time, but I think I'm right about this. It was across the way from the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, sir, you mentioned the division artillery group. Were there other artillery groups, and can you explain what weapons were available to the 12th Division within the city itself?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the Chamber to rule whether the general is allowed to use his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very practical for me to use so. It's slightly complicated, because I don't have my notes in electronic format. So there was the structure that was shown as the command structure with all of its elements. And then I also have this information here, reliable information, on combat equipment. If I may, I have a lot of information to share here, and I'd just like to specify the provenance if the Chamber allows, what the supply sources were, where all of this came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we need to explore that, Your Honour, because this is not about the general, with respect, testifying on the basis of his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no clue what the -- what general was referring to. It's for Mr. Karadzic to take up this, but -- yes, Mr. Milosevic, what document were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make one thing clear. I wanted to say what the indicators are telling me that the numbers here are true and that these numbers existed. If I may be allowed to explain that. You will receive an answer, because that will then tally with the previous confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question you were asked about is the artillery group, and in particular what weapons were available to the 12th Division within the city itself. So you can tell us what weapons were available, not necessarily the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may, General, sir, if I may assist. According to your records, according to your information, how many mortars, 80-millimetres, 62-millimetre -- 82-millimetre, 60-millimetre, and 122-millimetre mortars were there in the city itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can proffer some information that will corroborate this, if I may, just in order to follow a sequence that will confirm the existence of these figures. So if I may, if the Chamber can allow me to explain that I can move on to the figures afterwards because that is quite -- well, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear him out, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a story behind all of this. When the crisis first began in the former Yugoslavia and combat equipment was brought in from Croatia, from Slovenia, and from elsewhere, why was it being brought to Sarajevo? I don't know. What I do know is that it was now there. Specifically, it was now at the Marsal Tito Barracks at the Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks, and some of it went to Lukavica; meaning when the situation finally began to unravel, when certain areas were created under the control of this party or that party, then all this equipment at the Marsal Tito Barracks, Jusuf Dzonlic, Jajce, Victor Bubanj, all these military compounds, the weapons were kept there, held back, and ended up in the hands of the 1st BH Army Corps. All the companies that used to operate in existent peacetime, these were large-scale systems and they all had their anti-aircraft weapons or anti-aircraft weapon systems. That was part of the protection set-up. So everything that was there was now within the 1st Corps. In this case we're talking about the 12th Division, in a narrower sense. The more weapons that came in simply boosted these figures. Now there was this entire infrastructure in place in terms of accommodation, in terms of command, in terms of the supplies, logistics, repairs. This was all now in the hands of the 1st Corps. As for any military facilities that ended up in the hands of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there was only one such facility, Lukavica. It's also true that some of the equipment ended up in Lukavica and that was where it stayed. I'm talking about the equipment coming in from Croatia, Slovenia, and other territories across the former Yugoslavia. So when I say that there were six howitzers, 120 millimetre, it's a self-propelled weapon, these are the same howitzers that ended up in the Marsal Tito Barracks. So as soon as the men pulled out, students, pupils, secondary military school, military academy, and so on and so forth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything else that I'm talking about here are weapons that ended up in that area and they now had them. The weapons were available to them. Talking about anti-aircraft, PAT 20/1 and 20/3, these came from the previously operating civilian companies that I mentioned and these weapons were part of the erstwhile protection and defence set up. So if we put this all together, 60 millimetre, 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, there were between 140 [Realtime transcript read in error "100"] and 150 of those in the city itself. Howitzers, 122-millimetre, the self-propelled howitzer, six of those; 105-millimetre, three howitzers; T-55 tank, three of those; 130-millimetre gun, and to be quite specific, it was not in Sarajevo. It was on Mount Igman, and it was firing Sarajevo from Mount Igman because the range for that particular gun is over 30 kilometres; 76-millimetre gun called ZiS, it's a reference to Stalin. Four of those were available; recoilless cannons, 82-millimetres, we discovered that they had a total of 16 of those, but possibly many more than that that we didn't find. So when you fire this cannon, you can see it from miles away, because normally when it fires there's a plume of smoke rising from the gun. What I didn't say, all of the weapons of the special brigade for Yugoslavia. I'm talking about the MUP. I'm not sure what they called it at the time. There was this special brigade whose task it was to prevent terrorism. So this equipment was kept at a location known as Krtelj, which is right next to Donji Kotorac. Earlier on we said that the 104th Motorised Brigade was stationed there. So this was a selection of equipment, APCs, and what was known as Vidra. All of this was, in a manner of speaking, grabbed by the MUP, Sarajevo's police. Then it stayed there and was used as combat equipment. These are sophisticated weapons. These are wood weapons, and commanders were using these to drive across Sarajevo and not expose themselves to danger, although actually it was meant to be used by someone else, but that was a different matter altogether. So everything that I've been telling you about is in relation to 1994. I'm talking about this period and information telling us what weapons were available to the corps command, and then additional weapons started coming in for the 1st Corps in its entirety with equipment coming in from wherever, further afield, and their friends were helping. And these are the Crna Strela rockets, and the 9K11 rockets, and then 107-millimetre rockets, the so-called VBRs, multi-rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could we pause there. Could we see the memo or document you are looking at now with the assistance of the usher through the ELMO. I see the time. Shall we take a break now? In the meantime, you'd like at that take a look at the document, Ms. Edgerton, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it's what I think it is, the General's just read most of page 6 of his aide-memoire into the record, but I will take a look at it to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English, what page it would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Chamber receive that aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it did. The Serbian version is in the -- in the handwriting is page 11. It was sent by electronic -- it was sent out on Sunday electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What Chamber received is a document titled proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The exact situation is that you didn't receive the English. So only the Prosecution received that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I was asking. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.25. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understood the nature of the document you relied on, but where did you get those information, Mr. Milosevic, which is written on this document which we see now in front of us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- well, the information is the result the direct discovery of the existence of firing position and the fire from these weapons from the relevant firing positions from the Sarajevo area. This is one source of the information. This is through the observation system and by observing the existing weapons as they were firing and also while the weapons were being transferred from one firing position to another. This is one type of information. Then in the system of their documents, documents created by the commands that we're talking about from the 1st Corps or from the 20th -- 12th Division according to the type of fire they were planning and the actual firing that they executed, we worked out what their resources were in this sense at their disposal. There is a document. These are their original documents in which General Siber divided 100 mortars, 60-millimetre -- 160-millimetre mortars were distributed to the units. I really couldn't see that many, but it turns out that there were one hundred 60-millimetre mortars. I don't know if they fired or not. That's a different matter. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Just one matter. For the record, Mr. Milosevic, you referred to Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Dzambasevic. I take it his name is Dzambasovic, not s-e-v-i-c with last five letters s-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It appears on transcript page 4, line 16, 22, and 24. And he was one of the Prosecution witnesses, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, on page 66, line 10, I heard you say that there were between 140 and 150 mortars, but in the transcript it states between 100 and 150?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is what is written. That's what I should have said, and that's probably what I said, that there were between 140 and 150 mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I admire your thoroughness and I'm very grateful for that, but we really must now start dealing with conduct and actions and things like that. So we need to complete this as soon as possible. Are you able to tell us whether all of these resources were stationary or whether some of them were movable and would appear in several places and how was this done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My screen is not working. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have page 11 in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do have it. I thought that I had to see your questions on the monitor. All right. Very well. Thank you. It's quite clear that these were not stationary weapons. None of them were stationary and installed only in one place. It's a rule, it's a principle that weapons would change their firing positions because they would be discovered when they are used and so on and so forth. So some of them were stationary, some were not, but generally speaking, their positions would change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any mobile resources of large calibre that could be fired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were. I don't know if I should describe it as a major folly, but there were vehicle-mounted weapons. They would be fired, and then they would be moved away. I don't consider that to be warfare with any kind of logic or anything that would take into account the rules of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And these mobile assets, they were fired from which areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those assets often moved from the Zitomlin sector. This is the area of the Blagoje Parovic Street or possibly behind some larger buildings so that they would be less noticeable, but always you would notice if they were fired. In any case, they were mostly around the Blagoje Parovic Street. This is the new Sarajevo, centre of new Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to finish with this question of the deployment of forces, could you please tell me whose forces, for example, were in Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very important that I should give a clear answer to this question. This is the 104th Motorised Brigade that we're talking about here, which by its size was third largest brigade in that area. As for its combat assets, it was a brigade that had the greatest amount of these assets. That was the 104th in the area of Hrasnica, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and the eastern slopes of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could call up a map which we marked earlier with a witness, foreign witness, and then we could ask you to tell us whether the map correctly reflects who is where. Can we look at 1D32243, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you begin from the south?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us who was there. Who was in Dobrinja in that central area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 155th Mountain Brigade was in Dobrinja, and as I said it was under the command of Hadzic, Ismet Hadzic, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was at these elevations at Mojmilo Brdo and Hrasno Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 101st Mountain Brigade was there. That entire line was held by them from Hrasno Brdo all the way down to the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was at Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 115th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you're talking about brigades that were part of the 1st Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was at Jajce? What does that mean, Jajce, and who was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jajce is a barracks. It's a military facility. That's where the 152nd Brigade was. It was somewhat smaller in terms of its strength and Hilmo Kovac was in command. He was an officer that I admired highly, even in his conduct towards the enemy he was knightly, chivalrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you and who was at Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not managing to wait for this -- ah, all right. In Grdonj and in a broader area than that, but specifically at Grdonj the 105th Mountain Brigade was situated. It was under the command of Major Izet Bisevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the Grdonj and the disposition of the 105th Brigade, and how did that relate to Spicasta Stijena and the village of Mrkovici? Could you please mark the village of Mrkovici here on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, it's a satellite photograph, not a map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I mark this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can mark it in black because in the original we are -- already have markings in red and blue. Could you please mark Mrkovici and could you please tell us what -- the census of the events around Spicasta Stijena and Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to be able to pinpoint Spicasta Stijena here. All I can do is indicate the direction in which it could be in relation to the Grdonj location. This is here in this area, which has to do with the disposition of the 1st Corps. The forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were not at Spicasta Stijena. They were in the area of Mala Kula, and that area is behind Spicasta Stijena. And this is what -- is something that is being stated throughout the whole course of things that we were at Spicasta Stijena, but actually it's just a normal area, not a rock or a -- anything like that, and that's where the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you mark the village of Mrkovici with a number 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the word indicating the village of Mrkovici, but I know where it is. So it would be somewhere here. Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, General, sir, are you able to tell us briefly why in the reports Spicasta Stijena is mentioned so frequently? Mrkovici as well. What were the military activities there, and what was the purpose of the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key area that is of particular significance for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is the road leading from Pale via Sumbulovac to Vogosca, and then on to the rest of the front covered by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that road passes in the immediate vicinity of the village of Mrkovici. As for the 1st Corps, or, rather, the 12th Division, what was key was to attempt to cut off this road and in that way divide in two our front, one in the north-west and the other part would stay in the south, south-east or south-western area. So their activities were aimed via Spicasta Stijena at Mrkovici with the objective of severing the road and gaining a military advantage. Our situation did not permit us to lose this military advantage in terms of how we would live and function and carry out our combat activities. The attacks and the assaults were daily, and I'm not exaggerating when I say this. However, the minor ones are not that important. They attempted to break through with a considerably strong force, and then in the situation when they were prevented from doing that, then they would not report that somebody was firing at Sarajevo. They would say the Chetnik forces turned us back to our positions. So meaning that we fired at their positions and not at the city. This is one thing, an attempt to concentrate forces. So this main thrust was attempted on the 18th of September, 1994, and it was not only directed at Spicasta Stijena and the axis towards Mrkovici but other axes as well. This attack was prevented. It was stopped. I came to that place where there were soldiers attempting to break through, encountered some of our mines, and in one place I could see seven dead people there, men who were killed, and I couldn't help myself. Your Honours, if you believe me, I cried over those dead bodies. It was sending people to their death. That's what it was. Seven people in one place were beheaded. Their limbs were blown off in that mine explosion. And I asked myself, who is it that is sending those people towards us without any proper estimation? These people were not skilled for these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, who defended Mrkovici from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire -- the entire area between the Miljacka canyon where Miljacka flows into Sarajevo, as I mentioned earlier, via Hresa, and the positions at Mrkovici, Radava, Poljine, all the way to Rajlovac and the place where the Miljacka flows out of Sarajevo, all these positions were held by the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. That was the main force and the only force that held the entire north-west and part of the north-eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were these soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the members of the 3rd Brigade? Where were they from? Where did they hail from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just them when talking about the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, but this will imply to -- this will be true of all those who were in Sarajevo. They were all from the areas, for instance, from Vogosca, Rajlovac, Poljine, Mrkovici, Hresa, in other words -- from Bulog [phoen]. In other words, from those villages and the surrounding areas that were there. They were mobilised from there and became members of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please indicate on this image, this satellite image, where Sedrenik was vis-a-vis Grdonj and what military installations there were there if there were any, and what was the distance between Spicasta Stijena and your positions and Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first the area of Grdonj, that's the line that was covered by the 12th Division of the 1st Corps, and they had the 105th Brigade, which I mentioned earlier. Now, behind them or in there in their area was Hresa -- or rather, not Hresa but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where is Sedrenik? Could you mark it with an S on these slopes below Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be here approximately. This is the area right below Grdonj toward the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any snipers deployed at Spicasta Stijena, and would they have been in a position to open fire from Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. These are great distances, so it would be absolutely impossible to use any type of infantry weapons. You could only use artillery, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the artillery that was in Mrkovici village, what did they open fire at?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The artillery was withdrawn, was extracted from there, and it was placed under the command of UNPROFOR. It was centred in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my apologies. Mortar tubes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they too. And I'm talking about the period when UNPROFOR had made sure that all weapons would be placed under control. So the mortars were under their control as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please now go on. Let's take a look at Kobilja Glava, Hum, Zuc, and Sokolje. Who was in control of those hills or elevations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Hum was within the system of deployment of the city itself, except it was at a higher elevation. But Kobilja Glava and Zuc, let's talk about that. But there is no Orlic mentioned here or indicated here. And that was the highest elevation there between Kobilja Glava and Zuc, 800-something metres. Orlic, mount -- or a hill -- a peak, a mountain peak. This was the area that was under the control of the 112th Division -- or, rather, brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please indicate Orlic hill. What about Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to Sokolje. Orlic would be about here approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take that to be the letter O?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now could you just tell us who had control of Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Sokolje -- well, let me just make one thing clear. Sokolje was both a hill, and there was also a settlement, a place where people lived called Sokolje. And that was under the control of the 111th Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps -- or, rather, of the 12th Division. This position is dominant over Rajlovac, so the entire area of Rajlovac and the Sarajevo field are below these elevations such as Sokolje, Bresce Brdo, and so on and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have time now to ask you to mark Balino Brdo and Bresce Brdo, but --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here. It's right here, right next to Sokolje, Bresce Brdo, and I'll put a B there. But I don't see -- well, it's a bit lower than it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please date and sign this image in the bottom right, and could you tell us whether you would make any alterations to this image in terms of what areas were under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no need to make any alterations. I would just like to make it quite clear what the situation was with the Nedzarici area. It was in disastrous position. It was semi-surrounded and under attack, the objective being to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, at the beginning of your evidence today, you mentioned the intentions, the objectives of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honours. Just to note with respect to this document which I see is entitled in e-court "Annotated map based on Harland markings in court," Your Honours may recall -- well, in fact I direct Your Honours to page 2371 where there was a discussion of that map, and Mr. Tieger indicated on my behalf that the map which you now see in front of you is a map that included locations which were not only generally referenced by Mr. Harland but also additional locations requested by the accused. So I just wanted to make that clarification when I saw the title of the document. It's not necessarily reflective of locations marked by Harland at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember I encouraged some discussion and to reach an agreement, and I take it that such agreement has never been reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But we did engage in discussion in good faith, both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no problem admitting it as such?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that caveat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today on page 11, you mentioned the objectives, the intentions of the 1st Corps as well as the purpose of their activities. Could you tell us briefly what the intention of the 1st Corps of the BH Army was, and in particular, the objective of its -- the intention of its 12th Division, and that in relation to your area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no brief answer to this question, but I'll try to be as brief as I can. The intention was to break through the front line. Now, to be more specific, all operations that were directed through Nedzarici along that axis towards the west had the objective of linking up with airforces in Butmir and Hrasnica. Now, the forces that were in that area, our forces, my forces, they were exposed to constant and total barrage fire with the strongest assets. That's number one. And as far as we could assess the intentions of the enemy, and it's not difficult, it's easy to assess what an enemy's intentions are in a situation like this. Now, the next thing. The cutting off of the road that I mentioned earlier, the road between Pale and Vogosca, that action, that operation, was carried out on the eastward axis via Spicasta Stijena and Mrkovici, and that's where the road is. It's in the vicinity near Mala Kula where our forces were deployed. So if our forces were to be cut off there, then we would lose contact with several brigades. Next, there was an absolute attempt, and they did everything in their power, to cut off the communication leading toward Trnovo from the area of Mount Igman. In other words, from the positions from which the 104th Motorised Brigade engaged us. So if they were to cut off the road at Krupac, which was close to Vojkovici village, if that were to happen, we would lose that part of the front line, and we would have no access to it. The other operations that I could tell you about also had to do with attempts to cut us off in order to prevent us from moving and using our units along the axis between Semizovac towards Nisici. In the area of Srednje village they were in a dominant position which was 800 metres at an elevation of 800 metres, so this road was threatened, and if the road leading to Nisici were to be cut off, then our entire area of Ilidza would be cut off and completely surrounded, including Rajlovac, Hadzici, Vogosca, and Semizovici, not to mention what the situation like with Ilijas. So these were their general intentions, and they kept trying to resolve this and to get it done and finally they did with a Tekbir operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that -- the term temporarily taken or temporarily captured territory. What did that -- what meaning did that have in terms of their intentions? What was its significance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they legalised, as it were, or legitimised their own actions. So this was a temporarily taken position. This meant that whenever an area was defended and protected by where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had its forces, they considered that those were areas that they could legitimately put back under their own control. So this is the significance of the temporarily captured or -- territory. And I repeat that the original meaning of that was it was used in the event of a foreign aggression where people would have the right to defend themselves and there would be people living there, houses of Trapare and Ivcici and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what significance would this have on the entire war operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina had the 1st Romanija Corps -- the 1st BH Army Corps managed to break out of Sarajevo and move on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What that would mean? A disaster, a catastrophe. That was overambitious. It was not realistic. And there was an excess of attempts to make it seem as if nobody would be left with anything else, that everything belonged to them. I don't want to go into what belonged to whom, but I just know what the task of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. That was to defend the area where they were deployed. However, that is abundantly clear. Such a force, should it break through, would advance and overwhelm the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I would like to just point out here that it -- I'm not here in order to worry about the Republika Srpska -- or, rather, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' corps did not concern itself with the territory of Republika Srpska. Our job, our task was to defend that area where we were deployed. But were they to break through that would automatically jeopardise the rest of the territory. But I don't want to go further into that and elaborate, because had they managed to cut off the Rogoj Pass and connect, link up with Gorazde, then Herzegovina would have been lost. It would be cut off, and it would remain encircled. They would have encircled it. So that's how it was. In other words, you would have had to be a giant in order to be able to fight back and fight with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the consequences would have been for the immediate surroundings and the Serb villages around Sarajevo had the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps given in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours this is too broad a subject. I'm going to try and give you the basics on this and that have been quite a fine achievement given the time available to us. I'm talking about the area where there were people that we were meant to protect. They felt it would be a disaster were the corps to give in and allow an enemy incursion into our territory. People were pleading so much. People were trying to encourage us to persist and to do everything in our power to protect them from this incursion. People were living in fear, because were there to be a breakthrough by the enemy that would have meant their disappearance from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the enemy getting into Serb villages such as Cemerno and other villages? Did that fear felt by the population appear to be founded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever anything like that happened it caused suffering to the people on the receiving end. And it's more than just Cemerno, the area around the village and the village itself. I'm aware of that village for a different reason, not because I have direct experience. I received word at the time that people were killed there, that houses were burned, but the disaster that struck Velesici -- or, rather, Pofalici was in my opinion an even greater disaster. It was on the 15th of May, 1992. Were those military units or paramilitaries units, I don't know, but they were certainly extremists who got there, who set fire to houses and killed the locals there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the type of operations that the 1st Corps conducted in order to achieve these objectives? Can you tell us more about that? What type of combat operation? What type of offensive? What did you as a corps have to resist at your time as chief and later on at your time as corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the sheer variety of the operations unleashed against us, I can only congratulate them here or elsewhere. They devised their combat operations in a very clever way. All of the combat activities and operations that were launched in a tactical, operational and strategic sense we used. They used everything that was available. They tried to break through the lines. They tried to infiltrate and get behind our lines. They tried to use artillery. They used night-time combat as well. Sometimes we would find out in the morning that five of our men had been killed the previous night, men deployed at particular positions. So there was a variety -- variety of different operations and actions that they were using, sabotage operations, planting explosives, and so on and so forth. They were particularly good at sniping. I know the person who was in charge of devising this strategy. He's a highly skilled military officer. So he created this environment, and he ran the whole show. These activities and operations covered a particularly broad area, and this constituted an enormous danger to the safety of our own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you look at media reports or indeed when you look at evidence given before this Tribunal, one often mentions acts of provocation by the Muslims and our reaction to those taunts or acts of provocation. How do you distinguish between the two, the mere act of provocation on the one hand and a real combat operation on the other?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two were difficult to tell, and the intention behind each was difficult to distinguish, but we needed a working assessment in both cases, and we had to sort of decipher this for ourselves every time. It would have been irrational. It would have been needless to respond to provocation. So what we needed was reliable information indicating whether there was any serious intention of a military incursion, an attempt to break through our lines before we started firing back. Normally we did not rise to the bait. Obviously sometimes it was easy to tell, but we needed to exercise some caution in terms of our own assessments when assessing the intentions behind a particular move that they were making.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were brigade commander, did you know where they were, where their units and weapons were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I stated before this Chamber that we knew the enemy really well. We had them down to a T. But all this goes back to the initial stage in those early days when we all had to assess our own situations at our own basic level. So we knew where they were. We knew what they were doing, and we knew what their intentions were and what the danger involved for everyone was. And we had to go on studying the situation, obviously. The same thing that was done at brigade level was also studied elsewhere using certain methods, and then an assessment was drawn up at corps level in order to arrive at their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to show you a series of documents that you produced at the time. Therefore 65 ter 12446, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's also P4498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this has been admitted already, so we'll not be dwelling on this. You're talking about the disposition of enemy units; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Boljakov Potok right next to the supermarket. And then you mention all these locations, the skyscraper near the Kosevo pharmacy, Hrasno Brdo, Mojmilo, the Muslim Sandzak Brigade 900 to 1.000 men. And then you talk about Treska. What is this Treska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a building. There was a furniture shop there. It was a Skopje based company, a Macedonian company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned Zetra. What is Zetra?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a sports hall. It's a sports venue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Kosevo Hospital perimeter, there was a unit there that was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure it's necessary to go through all this information. It was information that we obtained in a variety of ways. So it's just information that was available to us at this initial stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in the Serbian please. Elementary school, medical school. You see what it says there. The use of civilian facilities and buildings such as schools and hospitals. To what extent did the 1st Corps resort to measures such as those using such civilian facilities and buildings for military purposes, that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything that was available, the facilities and buildings available within the city of Sarajevo, any possible purpose at all that these were used for. All of that was taken by the 1st Corps. Schools, hospitals, too, but let's not focus on that, because it was only Kosevo Hospital that they were using, not any of the other hospitals across the city. Nurseries, commercial buildings, shops, private homes, pubs. It was all covered. Had I been able to use such facilities in my capacity as commander in -- my position would have been a lot better than it was. So they had everything, all the facilities available to them, civilian, military and so on. Finally, when it came to the implementation of the Dayton Accords, their own authorities found it very difficult to persuade them to actually leave those facilities. The military had settled in and they ruled the roost, as it were. They refused to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, sir, but did they leave at least a single civilian area that would have been a safe place for civilians to stay inside Sarajevo and that did not comprise a single potential military target?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such areas in Sarajevo. I'll try and be more specific about this. If we're talking about a distance, say, 100 metres between a weapon and the troops there, then you can't consider that to be a civilian area, a safe civilian area. They did not have a choice but to use the space available in order to deploy their troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 1D07036, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you said that, say, a distance of 100 metres between a weapon and the troops there, and you can't consider that could be a civilian area. Does it mean that you can shell any part of the area, that being the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not allowed to shell a civilian area, nor indeed would we have chosen to shell a civilian area. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps didn't do that. Wherever there were civilians, that meant that was not a target for us. We never fired at those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean that you couldn't consider those area to be a civilian area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably misspoke in that sense, because that's not what I meant. What I'm trying to say -- if someone was a hundred metres away, that doesn't mean that this person is in an area that is exclusively civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is the command of the 1st Romanija Corps, the 1st of October. What are you doing there? You are simply rattling off a list of forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and then everything else that you see there: Bosna Transport, Prorad [phoen], Hrasno elementary school, faculty of architecture, Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing special to add. These locations that we identified were their collection points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in English please, and also the next page in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out loud the first paragraph from this page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might find that somewhat difficult: "At the railway station near the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, the medical school, the Kosevo stadium, the Marsal Tito Barracks, and the Victor Bubanj Barracks are deployed enemy artillery groups and individual artillery weapons. The artillery groups are of a mixed composition and strength, and they cover a broad area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber where, for example, this medical school used to be? Do you remember the exact location in relation to Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right. Right. These schools, the medical school, the secondary school for dentists and dental technicians, it's all within the Kosevo Hospital compound which was a large compound at Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you did not always respond to any -- every provocation. What was your reason not to respond to each provocation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not only that it was provocations. A response to their fire would often be no response not even when there was firing but it did not have the nature of a provocation. Those who are to use their weapons, and I'm talking from the position of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, had to secure a whole series of indicators in order to decide, to decide to open fire. The system of observation, all kinds of observation, observation of artillery, movements of the infantry, surveillance of the terrain, all of that was covered by our observation posts, and the observers had to provide information about what they were seeing and what was happening there and from which area did they open fire at us. One detail that occurred very often was that they would open fire at us, but they would fall below target because they use an insufficient charge or because the crews were not working properly, so the shells would fall short.
